# Introduction

In this report we analyze the incidence of colon cancer in Sweden across calender year as well as by age and sex. We do this with the goal of describing the incidence rate in different groups and with a particular focus on its development over calender year. We find that X

## Preamble: Loading data and initial set up

We begin by loading the data, and setting up the dataframes needed for the analysis.

```{r message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}

# Set up ------------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
#library(rms)
```

```{r message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Import and Clean Data --------------------------------------------------- 
cases_data <- read_tsv(
  "cases-2.tsv",
  col_types = cols(
    sex = col_factor(),
    year = col_double(),
    agegroup = col_factor(ordered = TRUE),
    n = col_double()
  )
)

population_data <- read_tsv(
  "population-2.tsv",
  col_types = cols(
    sex = col_factor(),
    year = col_double(),
    agegroup = col_factor(ordered = TRUE),
    n_pop = col_double()
  )
)

#Joins the two df by matching values on vectors and rename columns
merged_data <- full_join(cases_data, population_data) |> rename("n_cases" = "n")
```


## Question 1
We begin by exploring the number of colon cancer cases in each age group as well as by sex.
```{r question 1}
#aggregate no. cases for all years by age group and plot
merged_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = n_cases, y = agegroup, fill = sex)) + 
  geom_col(position = "dodge") + 
  labs(fill = "Sex", x = "Total Cases", y = "Age Group") +
  theme_minimal()
```
The graph tells us that the number of cases are greater in the older age groups. There are also some differences between males and females: females have a greater number of cases in the two oldest categories, while males, seemingly, have a greater number of cases in most other age groups. This sex difference needs further investigation, but will not be of main interest here.

## Question 2
Here we display the developmen of the number of cases over calendar years for men and women.
```{r question 2}
#plot the the total number of cases in each calendar year by males and
merged_data |>
```


## Question 6
```{r question 6}

# Aggregate cases and population by year and sex
total_data <- merged_data %>%
  group_by(year, sex) %>%
  summarise(
    total_cases = sum(n_cases),
    total_population = sum(n_pop),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Question 5 prerequisite
merged_data <- merged_data %>%
  mutate(
    incidence_rate = n_cases / n_pop,
    incidence_per_100000 = incidence_rate * 100000
  )

# Calculate incidence rates
total_data <- total_data %>%
  mutate(
    incidence_rate = total_cases / total_population,
    incidence_per_100000 = incidence_rate * 100000
  )

# Question 6: Plotting incidence rate per 100,000 of colon cancer over calender time
ggplot(total_data, aes(x = year, y = incidence_per_100000)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "blue"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~sex) +
  labs(
    title = "Colon cancer incidence rate over calendar year",
    x = "Calendar year",
    y = "Incidence rate per 100,000"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The incidence rate for colon cancer has generally been higher in women than in men in the data between 1970-2022, with this difference becoming smaller towards the end of the observed period. A portion of this could be attributed to the difference in age distribution between men and women, with women living 3.3 years longer than men on average in Sweden [@StatsSweden] and colon cancer being most prevalent in older age groups as observed in question 1. However, life expectancy alone cannot explain this difference. To determine whether women are more likely to develop colon cancer than men of the same age it would be necessary to compare the incidence rate between men and women of the same age or implement age-standardization and determine whether the difference is statistically significant. 

Incidence rates of colon cancer has been steadily increasing between 1970 and 2022, although this increase has not been monotone or uniform. Some reasons for this could include an ageing population, improvements diagnostic practices, and changes in disease risks. The average life expectancy in Sweden in 2022 has increased by 8.41 years from 1970 [@GlobalEcon]. Further analysis, especially age-standardization and a greater understanding of the provenance of the data is needed to infer whether colon cancer has been and is becoming more frequent.

## Question 7
```{r}
# Linear model, no interaction
model <- glm(
  total_cases~year + sex + 
    offset(log(total_population)), 
  family = poisson, 
  data=total_data)

# Linear model with interaction
model_linear <- glm(
  total_cases ~ year * sex + 
    offset(log(total_population)), 
  family = poisson,
  data = total_data
)

# Quadratic model
model_quadratic <- glm(
  total_cases ~ (year + base::I(year^2)) * sex + 
    offset(log(total_population)), 
  family = poisson, 
  data = total_data
)

# Cubic model
model_cubic <- glm(
  total_cases ~ (year + 
                   base::I(year^2) + 
                   base::I(year^3)) * sex + 
    offset(log(total_population)), 
  family = poisson, 
  data = total_data
)

# Compare model fit
AIC(model, model_linear, model_quadratic, model_cubic)

# Likelihood ratio tests
anova(model, model_linear, model_cubic, test = "Chisq")

summary(model_cubic)
```

The Poisson regression model was fitted as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(r) = {} & \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{year}
+ \beta_2 \text{year}^2 + \beta_3 \text{year}^3 \\
& + \beta_4 \text{sex}
+ \beta_5 (\text{sex} \times \text{year}) \\
& + \beta_6 (\text{sex} \times \text{year}^2)
+ \beta_7 (\text{sex} \times \text{year}^3).
\end{aligned}
$$

where $r$ is the incidence rate and males are the
reference group (male = 0, female = 1).

The year was modeled as a continuous variable, initially
assuming a linear relationship on the logarithmic scale,
while sex was included as a categorical variable with
male as the reference group. 

When comparing a main effects model and an interaction
model that took into account the potential differences
in incidence rate increases between males and females
over calendar years, a likelihood ratio test revealed
a significant improvement in the interaction model
($p=3.575\times10^{-7}$). Furthermore, the AIC was lower
by 23.9 in the interaction model (main effects = 1211.386,
interaction = 1187.475); therefore, the interaction model
was selected over the main effects model.

To assess whether a linear relationship between calendar
year and log incidence rate was appropriate, quadratic
and cubic polynomial models were also fitted. The cubic
model provided a significantly better fit than the linear
interaction model (likelihood ratio test: $p=1.425\times10^{-9}$).
The AIC decreased from 1187.475 to 1148.334,
suggesting that the improvement in model fit justified
the added model complexity.

The cubic model was therefore selected, allowing the
annual percentage change in incidence rate to vary
over calendar time and between sexes.

## Question 8
```{r question 8}
# Predicted crude colon cancer incidence rates per 100,000 individuals in 1970 and 2020,
# stratified by sex, using the Poisson regression model with a year--sex interaction.
pred_data <- expand.grid(
  year = c(1970, 2020),
  sex = c("Female", "Male"),
  total_population = 100000
)

pred_data$predicted_rate <- predict(
  model_cubic,
  newdata = pred_data,
  type = "response"
)

# Table

pred_data %>%
  select(year, sex, predicted_rate) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Year", "Sex", "Predicted incidence per 100,000"),
    caption = "Predicted crude colon cancer incidence rates"
  )

```
The calendar year was modeled as a continuous variable
and was assumed to have a cubic relationship with the
log incidence rate. This allows the annual percentage
change in incidence rate to vary over time for each sex.
The difference between males and females was taken
into account by including interactions between sex
and the polynomial terms of calendar year, allowing
the annual changes in incidence rate to differ
between males and females.

The Poisson regression model predicts an increase in
incidence rate from 28.43 to 51.09 per 100,000 women
and from 26.49 to 49.20 per 100,000 men between
1970 and 2020. The accuracy of these predictions
depends on the assumption that a cubic relationship
between calendar year and log incidence rate
appropriately describes the observed trends.

## Question 10:

To properly estimate the incidence rate of colon cancer while controlling for the confounding effect of an aging population, we fit age-specific Poisson regression model.

```{r question 10, eval = FALSE, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# 1. Create a numeric age index (1 to 18) corresponding to the 18 age groups (0-4 to 85-89)
merged_data$age_index <- as.integer(
  factor(
    merged_data$agegroup,
    levels = paste(seq(0, 85, 5), seq(4, 89, 5), sep = "-"),
    labels = 1:18
  )
)

# 2. Fit Candidate Model 1: Linear main effects (baseline model)
dd <- datadist(merged_data)
options(datadist = "dd")

m_linear <- Glm(
  n_cases ~ year + age_index + sex + offset(log(n_pop)),
  family = poisson(),
  data = merged_data, 
  x = TRUE, 
  y = TRUE
)

# 3. Fit Candidate Model 2: Add restricted cubic splines for non-linear effects of year and age
m_spline_main <- Glm(
  n_cases ~ rcs(year, 4) + rcs(age_index, 4) + sex + offset(log(n_pop)),
  family = poisson(),
  data = merged_data, 
  x = TRUE, 
  y = TRUE
)

# 4. Fit Candidate Model 3: Include Year x Age and Year x Sex interactions, excluding Age x Sex

m2 <- Glm(
  n_cases ~ rcs(year, 4) * (rcs(age_index, 4) + sex) + offset(log(n_pop)),
  family = poisson(),
  data = merged_data, 
  x = TRUE, 
  y = TRUE
)

# 5. Compare model fits using AIC to justify selecting the final model (m2)
AIC(m_linear, m_spline_main, m2)

# 6. View summary and knot placements for the final model
summary(m2)
# knot_placements <- specs(m2)
# print(knot_placements)
```


```{r}
# 1. Create a numeric age index (1 to 18) corresponding to the 18 age groups (0-4 to 85-89)
merged_data$age_index <- as.integer(
  factor(
    merged_data$agegroup,
    levels = paste(seq(0, 85, 5), seq(4, 89, 5), sep = "-"),
    labels = 1:18
  )
)

# 2. Fit Candidate Model 1: Linear main effects (baseline model)
m_linear <- glm(
  n_cases ~ year + age_index + sex + offset(log(n_pop)),
  family = poisson(),
  data = merged_data
)

# 3. Fit Candidate Model 2: Polynomial main effects (cubic for year and age)
m_poly_main <- glm(
  n_cases ~ year + base::I(year^2) + base::I(year^3) + 
            age_index + base::I(age_index^2) + base::I(age_index^3) + 
            sex + offset(log(n_pop)),
  family = poisson(),
  data = merged_data
)

# 4. Fit Candidate Model 3 (Final Model): Polynomials with Year x Age and Year x Sex interactions
m2 <- glm(
  n_cases ~ (year + base::I(year^2) + base::I(year^3)) * 
            ((age_index + base::I(age_index^2) + base::I(age_index^3)) + sex) + 
            offset(log(n_pop)),
  family = poisson(),
  data = merged_data
)

# 5. Compare model fits using AIC to justify selecting the final model (m2)
AIC(m_linear, m_poly_main, m2)

# 6. View the summary of the final model
summary(m2)



# 7. Compare models using an Analysis of Deviance (Likelihood Ratio Test)
anova(m_linear, m_poly_main, m2, test = "Chisq")
```

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(r) = {} & \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{year} + \beta_2 \text{year}^2 + \beta_3 \text{year}^3 \\
& + \beta_4 \text{age} + \beta_5 \text{age}^2 + \beta_6 \text{age}^3 \\
& + \beta_7 \text{sexFemale} \\
& + \beta_8 (\text{year} \times \text{age}) + \beta_9 (\text{year}^2 \times \text{age}) + \beta_{10} (\text{year}^3 \times \text{age}) \\
& + \beta_{11} (\text{year} \times \text{age}^2) + \beta_{12} (\text{year}^2 \times \text{age}^2) + \beta_{13} (\text{year}^3 \times \text{age}^2) \\
& + \beta_{14} (\text{year} \times \text{age}^3) + \beta_{15} (\text{year}^2 \times \text{age}^3) + \beta_{16} (\text{year}^3 \times \text{age}^3) \\
& + \beta_{17} (\text{year} \times \text{sexFemale}) + \beta_{18} (\text{year}^2 \times \text{sexFemale}) + \beta_{19} (\text{year}^3 \times \text{sexFemale})
\end{aligned}
$$
where $r$ is the incidence rate, males are the reference group (male = 0, female = 1), and age is indexed from 1 to 18 (age_index).

To estimate the colon cancer incidence rate while adjusting for population aging, we formulated and compared three Poisson regression models: a basic linear model, a polynomial main-effects model, and a full interaction model incorporating cubic polynomials for both calendar year and age index.

The final cubic interaction model was selected because it provides a superior fit. The AIC drops dramatically from 25,522.95 (linear model) and 13,481.46 (main-effects model) down to 12,950.72. Furthermore, the analysis of deviance confirms that the inclusion of the polynomial and interaction terms yields a statistically highly significant improvement ($p < 2.2 \times 10^{-16}$).

### Variable Modeling Rationale:

- **Calendar Year:** Modeled using a cubic polynomial ($\text{year}$, $\text{year}^2$, $\text{year}^3$) to capture non-linear temporal trends and inflection points over time.
- **Age:** Incorporated using a numeric index ($\text{age\_index}$, 1–18) transformed via a cubic polynomial, reflecting the non-linear, exponential increase in colon cancer risk among older cohorts.
- **Sex:** Included as a categorical variable to account for global baseline differences between males and females.
- **Interactions:** Year $\times$ Age and Year $\times$ Sex interactions were included to allow temporal trends to vary across age groups and between sexes, while the Age $\times$ Sex interaction was omitted to preserve model parsimoniousness.

```{r}
# Calculate Pearson dispersion statistic for the final model (m2)
(Pearson_disp_m2 <- sum(residuals(m2, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m2))
```

Also, by evaluating the Pearson residuals of our final model, we obtained a dispersion statistic of approximately **2.06**, which is notably higher than the value of 1 expected under a standard Poisson distribution. This indicates overdispersion in our data.

This imply that the model violates the standard Poisson assumption that variance equals the mean ($\text{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[Y]$); actual variance is roughly double, leading to underestimated standard errors. However, we retain standard Poisson because point estimates remain unbiased, and a dispersion of ~2.06 reflects mild-to-moderate overdispersion, a common occurrence in large-sample epidemiological count data due to unmeasured heterogeneity [@Cameron_Trivedi_2013].

## Question 11:

```{r question 11}
# Create a prediction data frame for specific years (1970, 2020), sexes, and age groups
pred_q11 <- expand.grid(
  year = c(1970, 2020),
  sex = c("Female", "Male"),
  age_index = c(11, 15, 18),
  n_pop = 100000
)

# Map age indices back to their corresponding factor labels for reporting
pred_q11$age_group <- factor(
  pred_q11$age_index,
  levels = 1:18,
  labels = paste(seq(0, 85, 5), seq(4, 89, 5), sep = "-")
)

# Predict the incidence rate per 100,000 individuals using the final model (m2)
pred_q11$predicted_rate <- predict(
  m2,
  newdata = pred_q11,
  type = "response"
)

# Format and display the results in a tidy table
pred_q11 %>%
  select(year, sex, age_group, predicted_rate) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Year", "Sex", "Age Group", "Predicted incidence per 100,000"),
    caption = "Predicted colon cancer incidence rates by age, year, and sex"
  )
```

The predicted incidence rates clearly illustrate that colon cancer risk increases exponentially with age, being dramatically higher in older cohorts (e.g., ~300 per 100,000 in the 85–89 age group) compared to middle-aged groups (~20–27 per 100,000 in the 50–54 age group). Furthermore, the rates consistently increased from 1970 to 2020 across all age categories and both sexes, reflecting rising overall temporal trends, with males generally exhibiting slightly higher predicted rates than females within the same age and year strata.

Calendar year and age were modeled using cubic polynomials to capture non-linear temporal trends and the exponential increase in colon cancer risk among older cohorts. Sex differences and temporal shifts were accounted for through baseline terms and a Year $\times$ Sex interaction. Additionally, a Year $\times$ Age interaction allowed time trends to vary across age groups due to changing diagnostics or risk exposures. Finally, the Age $\times$ Sex interaction was omitted to maintain model parsimoniousness, assuming consistent age-related risk structures across sexes.

## Question 12 

We age-standardize the incidence rates to take into account differences in the age distribution between calendar years. Here, we standardize the incidence rate with respect to age by year and sex, based on the sex-specific age-distribution in 2022.

```{r question 12}
# Q12 : Age-standardized incidence rates
data_2022 <- population_data |> 
  filter(year == 2022) |>
  select(sex, agegroup, n_pop_2022 = n_pop)

data_std <- merged_data |>
  mutate(incidence_rate = n_cases / n_pop) |>
  left_join(data_2022, by = c("sex", "agegroup")) |>
  group_by(year, sex) |>
  summarise(rate = sum(incidence_rate * n_pop_2022) / sum(n_pop_2022) * 100000, .groups = "drop_last" ) 
```

```{r question 12 plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=9}
plot_std <- ggplot(data_std, aes(x = year, y = rate)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "blue") +
  facet_wrap(~sex) +
  labs(title = "Age-standardized incidence rate of colon cancer over calendar year",
       x = "Calendar year",
       y = "(Age-standardized) Incidence rate per 100,000"
  ) +  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15))

plot_std
```

```{r question 12 comparison with 6, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5, fig.width=9}

# Comparison q6 vs q12
data_std <- mutate(data_std, analysis = "Age-standardized rate")
crude_data <- merged_data |>
  group_by(year, sex) |>
  summarise(rate = sum(n_cases) / sum(n_pop) * 100000, .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(analysis = "Crude rate")
comp_data <- bind_rows(crude_data, data_std)

comp_plot <- ggplot(comp_data, aes(x = year, y = rate, color = analysis)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~sex) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of age-standardized (Q12) vs crude (Q6) incidence rates",
    x = "Calendar year",
    y = "Incidence rate per 100,000",
    color = "Incidence rate analysis type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15)
  )
comp_plot
```

The obtained graphs show that the age-standardized incidence rate across years for men follows a similar but more moderate increase between 1970 and 2022 compared to the graph in question 6, whereas the age-standardized incidence rate for women is quite different. In the standardized graph, the curve is much flatter between 1970 and the 1990s before increasing moderately, in comparison to the continuous increase shown in question 6.

The apparent increase in colon cancer cases observed over the years, especially among women, thus seems to be largely due to the ageing of the Swedish population, rather than an increase in biological risk. As previously noted, it could be explained by overall increase in life expectancy in Sweden (increase of 8.41 years from 1970 to 2022 [@GlobalEcon]) but also by the fact that women live 3.3 years longer than men on average in Sweden [@StatsSweden]) and more prevalence for colon cancer in older age groups (observed in question 1).

## Question 13 
Both methods show that incidence increases over time for males and females. 
The model follows the overall trend. It does not capture all the (noisy) rises and falls
 including the sharper increase among females during the 2000s and 
the slower increase among males after around 2010

```{r model_standardised_rates_calculation, echo=FALSE}

predicted_rates <- expand.grid(
  year = sort(unique(merged_data$year)),
  sex = unique(merged_data$sex),
  age_index = sort(unique(merged_data$age_index)),
  n_pop = 1
)

predicted_rates$yhat <- predict(
  m2,
  newdata = predicted_rates,
  type = "response"
) * 100000

model_weights <- merged_data %>%
  filter(year == 2022) %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  mutate(weight = n_pop / sum(n_pop)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(sex, age_index, weight)

model_standardised <- predicted_rates %>%
  left_join(model_weights, by = c("sex", "age_index")) %>%
  group_by(year, sex) %>%
  summarise(
    ASR = sum(weight * yhat),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Combine with the direct estimates from Question 12.
comparison <- bind_rows(
  data_std %>%
    transmute(
      year, sex,
      ASR = rate,
      Method = "Direct standardisation"
    ),
  model_standardised %>%
    mutate(Method = "Regression model (m2)")
)
```

```{r model_standardised_rates_plot, echo=TRUE}
ggplot(comparison,
       aes(x = year, y = ASR, colour = Method)) +

    y = "Age standardised incidence per 100 000",
```

## Question 14 
Our modelling focused on how incidence changed over calendar time and whether these time trends
differed by age and sex. We therefore included age–year and sex–year interactions. 
We omitted the age–sex interaction to  focuse on time trends therefore the male to female rate ratio is assumed to be the same across ages within each year.
Without controlling for age the predicted male to female incidence rate ratio was $26.49/28.43 = 0.932$ in $1970$ and $49.20/51.09 = 0.963$ in $2020$. 
Ttherefore predicted crude incidence was about $6.8\%$ and $3.7\%$ lower among males, respectively. 
After controlling for age the corresponding ratios were 1.096 and 1.118, that is, higher predicted 
incidence among males at the same age.Their increase suggests a slightly greater  increase(statistical significance not verified) in incidence among males between these years.eventhough the graphs in Questions 6 and 9 suggest higher overall incidence among females
it does not imply higher incidence at the same age.

Non-standardised rates are useful when describing the actual incidence in a population.
 For example a healthcare planner could combine these rates with population size to estimate the  number 
 of colon cancer cases. Age-standardised rates are useful when comparing incidence across calendar years while holding
age composition constant. For example, comparing rates in 1970 and 2020 using the
